analysis.one_liner: Limits contractors' liability when construction workers are hurt in falls on federally funded projects.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Most states already decide injury cases by comparing each side's share of fault. New York, alone, holds property owners and contractors automatically liable when a construction worker is hurt in a fall, regardless of whether the worker ignored safety rules. This bill would bar that automatic liability on any project with federal funding — which covers nearly all major infrastructure work — and require courts to reduce a worker's recovery by their own share of fault. It applies to any person who works on, supervises, or is affiliated with such a project, and it covers workers hurt by falling loads as well as workers who fall.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners, contractors, and the insurers who underwrite their liability policies gain if the bill passes. It would cap their exposure on the most common and most expensive construction accidents — falls from heights and falling loads — and allow a worker's damages to be reduced or eliminated if the worker was partly at fault, such as by not using provided safety equipment. Supporters say lower liability costs would free money for construction and lower insurance premiums, particularly in New York.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Contractors, property owners, and liability insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans absolute liability for elevation and gravity-related injuries on any project using federal financial assistance, and requires a comparative negligence standard that accounts for the injured person's own conduct, including failure to use provided safety equipment or impairment by drugs or alcohol [S2] [S3].

The definition of 'project' covers highways, bridges, tunnels, airports, rail, transit stations, piers, and buildings that are federally owned or federally funded, and 'State' is defined broadly to include port authorities, transit agencies, and toll authorities — so the rule reaches nearly all major public infrastructure work [S3].
It applies retroactively in effect, reaching projects where federal assistance was accepted on or after January 1, 2021 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Injured construction workers bear the cost. Falls are among the leading causes of construction deaths and catastrophic injuries, and the workers at elevation are often low-wage laborers. Workers' compensation is preserved, but it does not pay for pain, suffering, or full lost earnings, so the bill would cut the recovery of workers who are hurt on the job and found partly at fault, while shielding the owners and contractors on the projects where they were injured [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill strips injured workers of full compensation in the cases where they are most often hurt: falls and falling loads on public works projects. A worker who was partly careless — or whom a jury finds partly careless — would see damages reduced even if the site conditions that caused the fall were the owner's responsibility [S2] [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that automatic liability is expensive: liability insurance for elevation work is a large cost for contractors, especially in New York, and those costs flow into bids on public projects. But the bill responds by shifting that cost onto the workers with the least ability to bear it, rather than by pairing the liability change with any safety requirement or wage protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings here go to contractors, owners, and insurers; the cost is borne by the workers who are hurt. Because falls from heights cause some of the most severe and most costly construction injuries, the shift in fault rules would fall on precisely the cases where workers most need compensation. There is no offsetting benefit to workers in the bill — no safety mandate, no wage provision, no training requirement — which makes this a straightforward transfer of injury costs from industry to labor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs (R-NY) introduced the bill on February 24, 2021, with Rep. Tom Reed (R-NY), and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S3] [S5].
On April 28, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no further action is listed, and it never reached the full committee or the floor [S5].
The bill's only cosponsors were two Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction contractors, property owners, and liability insurers are better off because the bill died: they continue to face full liability for elevation injuries on federally funded projects, and injured workers keep their current rights to recover.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractors' liability stays; workers keep full recovery

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Rep. Tom Reed
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer; the bill's only cosponsors were two Republicans.

for.name: Liability insurance and contractor trade groups
for.role: Industry supporters of scaling back absolute liability for elevation injuries
for.what_they_did: Campaign for years to replace automatic liability for construction falls with comparative fault, citing high insurance premiums on contractors, particularly in New York.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it was passed to a subcommittee on April 28, 2021, and died there.

against.name: Construction labor unions
against.role: Organized opponents of limiting the Scaffold Law-type liability
against.what_they_did: Oppose replacing automatic liability for elevation injuries with comparative fault, arguing it would let contractors shift blame onto injured workers and weaken site safety incentives.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; there is no record of any vote or floor action to measure broader support [S4].

industries.note: Insurers profit from liability premiums on construction work and pay the judgments when workers are hurt in falls. The bill would have reduced their payouts by allowing workers' own fault to cut their recovery — but as written, its death means insurers keep collecting full premiums on the current liability system.

The bill would have capped their exposure on fall and falling-load injuries, the most common and costly construction claims, by deducting the worker's share of fault. Its failure leaves their liability, and their incentive to keep sites safe, unchanged.

The bill would have reduced the recovery of injured workers on federally funded projects, which covers most major infrastructure work. Its death preserves workers' current rights, including the right to full compensation when a fall is caused by unsafe site conditions.
